title: Resilience Fund for Women 2026 Grants: Apply for Up to $50,000 in Flexible Funding for Women-Led Climate Resilience Organizations
summary: The Resilience Fund for Women has opened a new 2026 funding round offering US$15,000 to US$50,000 in flexible, unrestricted grants to eligible women- and non-binary-led community-based organizations working in Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, and Vietnam . The funding is designed for grassroots and community-based organizations whose work connects three critical areas: women’s health, safety and economic resilience; community-led climate adaptation; and communities connected to global value chains . Successful organizations will receive funding over a two-year period , giving them greater flexibility to strengthen existing programs, build institutional capacity, respond to changing community needs, deepen climate adaptation work, and invest in the long-term resilience of the women and communities they serve. Unlike many conventional funding opportunities that require organizations to design an entirely new project, this funding is unrestricted . Applicants do not have to create a standalone project solely for the grant. Instead, selected organizations can use the funding to strengthen, expand, deepen, or adapt their existing work according to their organizational priorities and the needs of the communities they serve. Phase 1 Application Deadline: 12 October 2026 Applications opened on 18 September 2026 and must be submitted through the official online application system. Organizations selected to proceed will be invited to a second application phase beginning around the end of October 2026, with final grant decisions expected in January 2027. About the Resilience Fund for Women The Resilience Fund brings together companies, foundations, women’s funds, civil society organizations, and women leaders to invest in the health, safety, wellbeing, economic resilience, and climate resilience of women and communities connected to global supply chains. The Fund seeks to move resources and decision-making closer to women-led and community-based organizations that understand the realities facing their own communities. Its funding model differs from many conventional philanthropic approaches because it emphasizes: Flexible funding Long-term organizational resilience Trust-based philanthropy Community leadership Participatory grantmaking Women’s leadership Language accessibility Shared learning Community-led solutions Collaborative approaches to defining and measuring impact Rather than requiring grantees to follow rigid funding structures designed entirely by donors, the Fund aims to provide organizations with greater freedom to determine how resources can be used most effectively. A Funding Model Focused on Local Women-Led Solutions The Resilience Fund was developed around the principle that communities closest to social, economic, health, and environmental challenges are often best positioned to determine appropriate solutions. The Fund therefore provides flexible, multi-year support that allows community organizations to respond to changing circumstances rather than being restricted to a narrow project plan. This approach allows organizations to make decisions about where resources can create the greatest impact, including investing in organizational systems, staffing, existing programs, emerging priorities, or new approaches to climate adaptation. The Fund also uses participatory grantmaking, bringing community representatives into the process of assessing applications and influencing funding decisions. Funding Available Under the 2026 Resilience Fund Round Eligible organizations may request between: US$15,000 and US$50,000 in total funding. All grants awarded during this funding cycle will cover a: Two-year period. The grants are intended to provide organizations with longer-term and flexible support rather than short-term emergency assistance. Maximum Grant Relative to Organizational Revenue An important rule applies to the size of the grant that an organization may request. Applicants may request funding equivalent to up to 150% of their organization s annual revenue , subject to the overall maximum grant of US$50,000. For example, an organization with most recent annual revenue of US$20,000 could request up to: US$30,000 because this represents 150% of its annual revenue. Even if 150% of an organization s revenue would exceed US$50,000, the maximum available grant remains US$50,000 . Organizations must have annual income of at least US$10,000 to qualify. Income from 2024, 2025, or 2026 may be used as the baseline for determining eligibility. Three Priority Areas for the 2026 Funding Round The Resilience Fund is seeking organizations whose work brings together three interconnected areas . Applicants should demonstrate that their work addresses all three areas, although they are not expected to have the same depth of experience in each one. 1. Women’s Health, Safety and Resilience The first priority area concerns work that strengthens women’s overall wellbeing and their ability to participate fully in their workplaces and communities. Relevant work may address areas such as: Women’s health Safety Livelihoods Financial security Leadership Decision-making Mobility Economic participation Workplace wellbeing Community participation Resilience to economic or social shocks The objective is to strengthen conditions that allow women to live safely, build economic security, exercise greater agency, and participate meaningfully in community and workplace life. 2. Community-Led Climate Adaptation The second priority is work that helps women and their communities prepare for, respond to, and adapt to environmental and climate-related impacts. Examples of relevant climate risks include: Extreme heat Flooding Drought Storms Changing rainfall patterns Changing weather conditions Environmental degradation Climate-related livelihood disruption The Fund recognizes that climate impacts are not gender-neutral. Environmental shocks can affect women disproportionately through changes in working conditions, health risks, safety, migration patterns, income security, care responsibilities, and access to essential services. The Fund therefore aims to support locally designed climate adaptation strategies that place women and community leadership at the center of resilience building. Organizations Do Not Need to Be Long-Established Climate Organizations One particularly important aspect of this funding round is that applicants do not need many years of experience running formal climate programs. Organizations that are still in the early stages of incorporating climate adaptation into their work may apply. Applicants should, however, be able to demonstrate: Some existing experience responding to environmental or climate impacts affecting their communities; and An interest in strengthening or deepening climate adaptation within their work. The Fund specifically states that applicants do not need to identify primarily as climate-focused organizations. This provision may significantly broaden access to the funding for grassroots women’s rights, worker rights, health, economic empowerment, migration, safety, or community organizations that increasingly encounter climate-related challenges through their existing work. 3. Connection to Global Value Chains The third essential component is a connection to global value chains . For the purposes of this funding round, the Fund is particularly interested in organizations working with communities located in, near, or connected to businesses and workplaces producing products for global export. These can include sectors involving: Apparel Food Agriculture Technology Manufacturing Other export-oriented industries Relevant communities can include women who are: Factory workers Farm workers Migrant workers Informal workers Gig workers Organizations can also work with the families and communities surrounding these workers. The Fund s definition is intentionally broad. Organizations do not necessarily have to work directly inside factories or formal workplaces. They may work in communities surrounding manufacturing or agricultural operations or in communities from which women migrate significant distances for employment. Why Global Supply Chains Matter to the Fund Millions of women across South and Southeast Asia participate directly or indirectly in global supply chains. Their economic opportunities can be influenced by workplace safety, healthcare access, mobility, environmental conditions, gender-based violence, migration, extreme weather, and changing economic circumstances. The Resilience Fund s approach recognizes that improving women’s workforce participation cannot be separated from their health, safety, family wellbeing, community resilience, and ability to respond to climate risks. Supporting women-led community organizations can therefore strengthen both individual workers and the broader communities upon which global value chains depend. Who Can Apply? The 2026 funding round is open to eligible: Women- and non-binary-led, community-based, non-governmental organizations operating in: Bangladesh Cambodia India Vietnam Organizations must be formally registered and should be embedded in and representative of the communities they serve. Applicants must also meet the Fund s financial and regulatory requirements. Organization Registration Requirements Applicants must generally be: Formally registered organizations Non-governmental organizations Community-based Legally authorized to operate Legally authorized to receive foreign funding Organizations also need to comply with applicable government regulations governing foreign financial support. Minimum Organizational Income Applicant organizations must have annual income of at least: US$10,000 The Fund may use income figures from 2024, 2025, or 2026 to assess this requirement. Requirements for Women- and Non-Binary-Led Organizations The Resilience Fund places women s and non-binary leadership at the center of this funding cycle. Its current eligibility guidance describes a women/non-binary-led organization as having a woman or non-binary Executive Director or CEO and at least 50% of staff identifying as women or non-binary . The application page additionally describes its definition of a women-led organization as having a woman CEO or director and at least 50% of senior leadership positions held by women . Organizations close to, but not obviously within, these definitions should carefully review the official application guidance. The Fund states that an organization that believes it is genuinely women-led despite not precisely matching the stated definition may provide supporting information for consideration. Inclusive Understanding of Women The Fund states that the term women includes women in all their diversity. This encompasses, among others: Women with disabilities Women of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities Women of color Indigenous women Women from oppressed castes Younger women Older women Women affected by racism Women affected by poverty Migrant women Women belonging to other marginalized communities This reflects the Fund s broader emphasis on intersectionality and community representation. Foreign Funding Authorization Requirements Organizations generally must possess the legal approvals necessary to receive foreign funding. The Fund states that organizations without the required foreign funding authorization are generally not eligible . Special Provision for Applicants in India Without FCRA Registration There is an important exception affecting Indian applicants. For eligible organizations in India without an existing Foreign Contribution Regulation Act (FCRA) authorization, the Fund states that if the grant application is successful and the organization chooses to submit a prior-permission request to the Government of India, the Resilience Fund team can support the organization with that process. Indian organizations should carefully review the official funding and FCRA requirements before applying. Previous Resilience Fund Grantees Can Apply Again Organizations that have already received funding from the Resilience Fund are allowed to apply during this round. However, previous receipt of a grant does not guarantee future selection. Returning organizations must: Meet the current eligibility requirements Submit a new application Participate in the current selection process Be evaluated alongside other eligible applicants All proposals will be reviewed under the same selection process. No New Standalone Project Is Required Organizations do not need to design a completely new project to qualify for this funding opportunity. This is one of the most important characteristics of the grant. The funding can be used to: Strengthen existing work Deepen existing programs Adapt existing interventions Develop organizational capacity Integrate climate adaptation more intentionally Respond to changing community priorities Strengthen internal systems Support programmatic needs Address institutional priorities Applicants will be asked to explain how they expect to use the funding and what they hope the support will allow them to achieve. What Does “Unrestricted Funding” Mean? The Resilience Fund describes its grants as flexible and unrestricted. This means selected organizations will have considerable discretion to determine where funding can best strengthen their organization and mission. Funds may potentially support both: Programmatic needs; and Organizational needs. Rather than requiring every dollar to be tied to a predetermined project budget, organizations can adjust the use of funding when circumstances or community needs change. This type of funding is particularly valuable for smaller grassroots organizations, which often face difficulty obtaining funding for essential institutional costs. Restrictions on Grant Funding Although the grants are flexible, they are not completely without restrictions. Grant funds cannot be used for : Lobbying Electioneering Political campaigning Microcredit Microfinance All grant funds must also be used in accordance with applicable national laws, foreign-funding regulations, and the terms of the final grant agreement. Two-Phase Application Process Applications will be assessed through a two-stage selection process . This structure is intended partly to prevent smaller organizations from having to invest substantial time in a highly detailed proposal before knowing whether their application is competitive. Phase 1: Initial Application Opening Date: 18 September 2026 Deadline: 12 October 2026 Organizations submit an initial application containing the information required to determine eligibility and assess alignment with the Fund s priorities. Applications will then undergo screening and review. A selected group of organizations will be invited to continue to Phase 2. Phase 2: Detailed Application Phase 2 is expected to: Open: End of October 2026 Close: Mid-November 2026 Organizations invited to this stage will provide more detailed information regarding: Their organization Their work Programmatic activities Proposed use of grant funding Relevant organizational and program details Organizations invited to Phase 2 are expected to be notified by the end of October 2026 . Final Funding Decisions Final grant decisions are expected to be communicated in: January 2027 All applicants will be informed of the final funding decision. Organizations selected for funding will then proceed through additional due diligence. This can include: Additional organizational information Reference checks Compliance review Grant documentation Signing a grant agreement The exact grant-processing timeline may differ according to legal and regulatory requirements in each country. Participatory Grantmaking Process A distinctive element of the Resilience Fund is its approach to deciding which organizations receive funding. Instead of leaving grant decisions entirely to conventional donor staff, the Fund uses participatory grantmaking . Eligible proposals progressing through the process are reviewed with involvement from community representatives and peer reviewers. Peer Panelists can include: Local gender activists Labor activists Value-chain experts Representatives familiar with relevant communities The Fund states that final grantmaking decisions are made through collaborative workshops involving Peer Panelists, Advisory Board members, and members of the Fund s operations team. The intention is to give people with community knowledge and lived experience a meaningful role in deciding how financial resources are distributed. Learning Hub for Successful Grantees Organizations selected for funding will also join the Resilience Fund Learning Hub . The Learning Hub is designed to connect: Grantee organizations Corporate investors Women s funds Community organizations Civil society organizations Fund stakeholders Participants can share experiences, examine challenges, exchange resources, identify lessons, and create new professional relationships. Over the two-year grant period, grantee organizations are expected to participate in approximately three to four virtual meetings with other grantees, investors, and Fund stakeholders. Translation and other support are intended to help participants communicate as much as possible in their preferred languages. Reporting Requirements The Fund states that reporting for selected grantees will be intentionally light-touch . Rather than imposing an identical set of fixed indicators on every organization, the Fund plans to collaboratively develop metrics and learning priorities with its grantee partners. This recognizes that organizations: Operate in different contexts Address different community priorities May define impact differently May require different approaches to measuring progress The Fund therefore emphasizes learning and useful information rather than imposing unnecessarily burdensome reporting systems. Application Language The final application must be submitted in: English However, applicants can access free application and language assistance . Support is available in languages including: Bengali/Bangla Hindi Tamil Khmer Vietnamese Odia Marathi Support can include assistance with translating application responses and submitting the application. The Fund states that applicants who receive language or application assistance will be assessed in the same way as applicants who complete their applications without such support. Application Support Contacts Applicants from India and Bangladesh can seek application assistance through the support arrangements listed on the Fund s official page. Applicants from Vietnam and Cambodia can similarly access language and application support through the Resilience Fund. Candidates should consult the official application page for the latest support contact information and translated application materials. Informational Webinar The Resilience Fund has scheduled an informational webinar for: 30 September 2026 at 8:30 a.m. EST Prospective applicants can register through the link provided on the official funding page. Organizations considering an application may benefit from attending the webinar, particularly if they have questions about eligibility, grant size, climate adaptation requirements, unrestricted funding, or the application process. Applications Must Be Submitted Online The Resilience Fund will accept only applications submitted through its official online portal . Applications cannot be submitted: By email On paper Through alternative offline arrangements Applicants with connectivity problems are encouraged to seek application support. Applicants Can Save Their Progress Organizations do not have to complete the online application in a single session. The online system allows users to save progress and return later using the same email address. The Fund recommends drafting application answers in a separate document before copying them into the application system. This can reduce the risk of losing work because of connectivity or browser problems. Application Confirmation After successfully submitting an application, applicants should receive an email containing confirmation and a copy of their submitted responses. The Fund asks applicants not to submit multiple applications for the same organization. What Happens If Your Organization Is Selected? Successful organizations will undergo a short due-diligence process. This can include: Verification of organizational information Reference checks Regulatory review Completion of grant documentation Once due diligence has been completed, successful organizations will receive a formal grant agreement. After signing the agreement, grantee partners will be introduced to the Resilience Fund s Learning Hub through an orientation process. The Fund also plans individual conversations with participating organizations to understand: How they define impact What they want to learn Their organizational objectives Their learning priorities The Resilience Fund’s Track Record The Fund has already developed a substantial portfolio of support for women-led and community-focused organizations. Since 2021, the Resilience Fund reports investing approximately US$4.27 million in 66 direct and indirect grantee partners , primarily in Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, and Vietnam. Its grantees work with groups including: Industrial workers Agricultural workers Migrants Children and families of workers Formal workers Informal workers Community members The Fund evaluates its broader impact across organizational resilience, learning, and philanthropy. Why This Funding Opportunity Is Different The Resilience Fund s 2026 funding round stands out because it combines several features that are often difficult for grassroots organizations to find in a single funding opportunity. These include: Two years of funding Flexible and unrestricted support Grants of up to US$50,000 Support for existing work rather than only new projects Opportunities for relatively early-stage climate-adaptation organizations Community-led decision-making Participatory grantmaking Language support Reduced reporting burden Organizational development support Peer learning Connections with other grantees and investors The combination is intended to strengthen not only individual projects but also the organizations delivering them. Key Dates at a Glance Phase 1 Opens: 18 September 2026 Informational Webinar: 30 September 2026 Phase 1 Application Deadline: 12 October 2026 Phase 2 Opens: End of October 2026 Phase 2 Deadline: Mid-November 2026 Final Funding Decisions: January 2027 Grant Duration: Two years Grant Amount: US$15,000–US$50,000 How to Apply for the Resilience Fund for Women 2026 Grant Organizations interested in applying should first carefully review the full eligibility requirements. Applicants are encouraged to download the application form in advance and prepare their responses before beginning the online submission. The recommended process is: Confirm that the organization operates in Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, or Vietnam. Confirm that it satisfies the women/non-binary leadership requirements. Confirm formal NGO registration. Check foreign-funding authorization requirements. Confirm annual organizational income of at least US$10,000. Confirm that the organization s work relates to women’s health, safety, and resilience. Demonstrate existing or emerging work on community-led climate adaptation. Demonstrate a connection with communities involved in global value chains. Review the application questions in advance. Prepare responses offline. Submit the Phase 1 application through the official online portal before 12 October 2026. Only applications submitted through the online application portal will be considered. Official Funding Information and Application: https://www.resiliencefundforwomen.org/apply Conclusion The Resilience Fund for Women 2026 funding round represents a major opportunity for women- and non-binary-led grassroots organizations in Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, and Vietnam that are working at the intersection of women s wellbeing, climate resilience, and global supply-chain communities. Selected organizations can receive between US$15,000 and US$50,000 in flexible, unrestricted funding over two years , giving them the ability to strengthen their existing programs and institutions rather than being forced to create a new standalone project solely to satisfy donor requirements. The Fund is particularly relevant for organizations working with women workers, migrant communities, informal workers, factory communities, agricultural workers, and communities affected by increasing climate and environmental risks. Its participatory grantmaking structure, flexible funding model, Learning Hub, language support, and light-touch reporting system distinguish it from more conventional project-based funding opportunities. Organizations do not need decades of experience in climate programming. Groups beginning to integrate climate adaptation into existing work are explicitly encouraged to apply if they can demonstrate some experience responding to climate or environmental challenges and a commitment to deepening this work. Interested organizations should review the eligibility conditions carefully and submit their Phase 1 application through the official portal no later than 12 October 2026 . title: NYCI Project Officer – Global Citizenship Education Trainer 2026: Apply for a €35,779–€48,408 Role in Dublin
summary: The National Youth Council of Ireland (NYCI) is accepting applications for a Project Officer: Global Citizenship Education Trainer , an opportunity for an experienced education, training, youth work, or global citizenship professional to contribute directly to the organisation’s Youth 2030 Global Youth Work Programme . Based in Dublin, Ireland , the full-time position combines training and facilitation, educational resource development, project coordination, stakeholder engagement, monitoring and evaluation, and work supporting the integration of Global Citizenship Education and Global Youth Work across Ireland’s youth sector. The successful candidate will join the Youth 2030 team and contribute to efforts to ensure that young people become better informed about global challenges and more actively engaged in advancing the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) . The position comes with an annual salary of €35,779 to €48,408 , depending on qualifications and experience, together with hybrid working arrangements, 27 days of annual leave, pension contributions, professional development opportunities, family-friendly working provisions, and a range of additional employee benefits. Application Deadline: 2:00 p.m. on Monday, 28 September 2026 Applicants should note that NYCI’s general vacancy announcement gives a later deadline of 5:00 p.m. on the same date, but the organisation’s live recruitment and application page states 2:00 p.m. on Monday, 28 September 2026 . Candidates are therefore strongly advised to treat 2:00 p.m. as the effective deadline and submit well before that time. About the National Youth Council of Ireland The National Youth Council of Ireland works to support and strengthen the youth sector in Ireland while promoting policies, services, programmes, and opportunities that improve the lives of young people. Its work spans areas including youth work, global youth work, equality and intercultural engagement, youth health, international engagement, digital youth work, youth arts, child protection, advocacy, education, and professional development. For professionals passionate about youth participation, equality, sustainability, social justice, global issues, and education, working with NYCI provides an opportunity to contribute to programmes capable of influencing practice across the wider youth sector. The organisation also places significant emphasis on creating an inclusive workplace and states that it values different identities, perspectives, and experiences while providing opportunities for staff learning and professional growth. About the Youth 2030 Global Youth Work Programme The successful Project Officer will work within Youth 2030 , NYCI’s major Global Youth Work and Development Education programme. Youth 2030 is funded by Irish Aid and is intended to increase the integration, quality, and reach of Global Youth Work and Development Education throughout non-formal youth work organisations, programmes, and projects. The programme is led by the National Youth Council of Ireland as part of a consortium involving Concern Worldwide, Trócaire, and Maynooth University . At its core, Global Youth Work encourages young people to understand both their role within their local communities and their connection to an increasingly globalised world. It gives young people opportunities to examine complex global issues including: Poverty Inequality Hunger Injustice Climate change Sustainable development Global interconnectedness Social and economic justice Equality International development Rather than simply presenting information about these challenges, Global Youth Work seeks to encourage critical thinking, participation, and action among young people. Purpose of the Project Officer: Global Citizenship Education Trainer Role The Project Officer will play a key role in delivering the outcomes of NYCI’s Youth 2030 Global Youth Work Programme. A central objective is ensuring that Global Youth Work becomes more fully integrated into non-formal youth work programmes and activities carried out by NYCI member organisations and the wider youth sector. The programme aims to help young people become better informed about global challenges while empowering them to become active participants in efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030. The role will also contribute to ensuring Global Youth Work is incorporated into professional youth and community work training at third-level education institutions . Another important area of work involves supporting innovation, research, and capacity development throughout the youth sector. This includes identifying and responding to challenges and opportunities that can broaden and deepen Global Youth Work, while developing stronger connections with the Global South. Main Responsibilities of the Project Officer This is a diverse role involving training, project administration, resource development, stakeholder engagement, monitoring, evaluation, and external representation. Planning and Delivering Global Citizenship Education Training One of the most significant responsibilities will involve working with Youth 2030 colleagues to identify training needs throughout the youth sector. The Project Officer will then help plan, coordinate, design, and deliver workshops and training interventions addressing those needs. Training will be delivered at different levels of the youth sector, meaning the successful candidate will need to adapt material and facilitation methods to different audiences and professional contexts. Training delivery will take place through both in-person and virtual formats , while bespoke training may also be designed in response to specific organisational requirements. Managing Training Administration The position is not restricted to facilitation. The successful applicant will also be responsible for administrative processes associated with training activities, including management of the programme’s training booking system. Effective administration will therefore be important for ensuring that programmes are properly scheduled, coordinated, communicated, and delivered. This means candidates should be comfortable moving between outward-facing facilitation responsibilities and detailed administrative work. Developing Educational Resources Another significant responsibility involves devising and developing educational resources for Ireland’s youth sector. These resources can help youth workers, educators, organisations, and young people engage more effectively with Global Citizenship Education, sustainable development, global justice, and related issues. The role therefore provides an opportunity for someone with experience translating complex social or global issues into accessible learning materials. Educational resource development is particularly important because Youth 2030 seeks not only to deliver individual training sessions but also to strengthen the long-term capacity of youth workers and youth organisations. Supporting the Global Youth Work Educators Network The Project Officer will facilitate and support the Global Youth Work Educator’s Network . Professional networks can provide important opportunities for educators and practitioners to exchange experiences, learn from one another, identify emerging challenges, develop good practice, and improve the overall quality of Global Youth Work. The successful candidate will therefore need strong facilitation and relationship-management abilities alongside technical knowledge of Global Citizenship Education and youth work. Building Relationships Across the Youth Sector Stakeholder engagement represents another major dimension of the position. The Project Officer will engage with NYCI member organisations and with the broader youth and Development Education community. This will involve maintaining relationships with existing stakeholders while potentially developing new connections and collaborative opportunities. The work may include interaction with youth organisations, educational institutions, trainers, educators, youth workers, community organisations, development organisations, and other actors involved in Global Citizenship Education and Global Youth Work. Contributing to the Youth 2030 Team The successful applicant will become an integral member of the NYCI Youth 2030 Global Youth Work team. They will contribute both to the specific objectives of the Youth 2030 programme and to implementation of NYCI’s wider strategic direction. This means the role requires someone capable of looking beyond isolated training activities and understanding how individual projects, resources, partnerships, and capacity-building initiatives contribute to wider organisational outcomes. The Project Officer will work toward the objectives established within the Youth 2030 Global Youth Work Results Framework while contributing to the delivery of NYCI’s Strategic Plan. Monitoring, Evaluation and Impact Measurement Monitoring and evaluation forms a defined part of the role. The Project Officer will work with other staff to implement the programme’s monitoring and evaluation framework and help assess the effectiveness and impact of Youth 2030 activities. This may involve gathering evidence, reviewing programme outcomes, assessing training effectiveness, analysing feedback, and contributing information that helps the organisation understand whether its interventions are creating the intended results. This dimension makes the position particularly interesting for professionals who combine training and facilitation experience with an interest in evidence-based programme management. NYCI’s original vacancy announcement specifically asks whether prospective candidates have experience using monitoring and evaluation tools, demonstrating the importance of this capability to the position. External Representation The selected candidate will also represent Youth 2030 externally within Global Citizenship Education arenas . External representation may involve engaging with professional networks, partner organisations, educational institutions, development-sector stakeholders, youth organisations, and other communities involved in Global Citizenship Education. As a result, the successful applicant will be expected to represent NYCI and Youth 2030 professionally while communicating effectively with different audiences. Contribution to Sustainable Development Goals The position has a particularly strong connection with sustainable development. Youth 2030 aims to ensure that young people become more informed about global challenges and more active in helping achieve the Sustainable Development Goals by 2030. Through training, education, capacity building, youth participation, and resource development, the Project Officer will therefore contribute to creating greater awareness of issues connected with global justice, sustainability, climate change, inequality, and development. The position provides an opportunity to translate the SDGs from international policy frameworks into practical youth education and engagement activities. Training and Continuous Professional Development Training and continuous professional development are established elements of NYCI’s Global Youth Work activities. Youth 2030 provides tailor-made training designed to strengthen the knowledge and practical capabilities required to deliver high-quality Global Youth Work. The wider programme also supports learning through initiatives including online education, professional development activities, and educational programmes developed with partner institutions. The Project Officer will therefore operate within an established training ecosystem rather than developing activities in isolation. Location and Working Arrangements The position is based at: National Youth Council of Ireland 3 Montague Street Dublin 2 Ireland Travel will be required as part of the role. NYCI is also currently operating a hybrid working model , which provides some flexibility between office-based and remote work. Candidates should nevertheless understand that this is not advertised as a fully remote position. The role involves in-person training, stakeholder engagement, travel, and other professional responsibilities requiring physical presence. Working Hours The position is full-time and involves: 35 hours per week Some flexibility will be required, including the possibility of working during evenings and weekends when programme activities require it. Applicants should therefore consider whether they can accommodate occasional working patterns outside conventional office hours. Contract Duration The position is offered on a one-year contract running to December 2027 . There is potential for the contract to be extended, but any extension will be dependent on continued funding. The recruitment documentation describes the appointment as a specified-purpose contract . This means applicants should not interpret the vacancy as an automatically permanent appointment. Salary The advertised annual salary range is: €35,779 – €48,408 per annum The actual salary offered will depend on the successful applicant’s qualifications and relevant professional experience. This gives experienced candidates some scope to enter above the bottom point of the advertised salary range, subject to NYCI’s assessment and applicable employment arrangements. Employee Benefits NYCI provides employees with a substantial package of benefits and professional supports intended to contribute to financial security, personal wellbeing, professional development, and work-life balance. Benefits listed for this position include: 27 days of annual leave Access to sick leave arrangements Parental leave schemes Bereavement leave provisions Employee Assistance Programme Death-in-service benefit equivalent to four times salary Family-friendly flexible working hours Hybrid working arrangements Tax Saver commuter ticket arrangements Cycle to Work Scheme Staff supervision Staff training and professional development opportunities Pension contributions NYCI states that these benefits and supports are intended to enhance staff wellbeing and promote a healthy balance between professional and personal responsibilities. Support for Candidates Attending Interviews NYCI has introduced a practical measure intended to reduce financial barriers for applicants attending face-to-face interviews. Candidates invited to attend an in-person interview may receive reimbursement for public transport costs within Ireland , subject to providing receipts. The organisation specifically connects this measure with the financial challenges that people on lower incomes can experience when attending interviews and with wider cost-of-living pressures. Child Safeguarding Responsibilities Because the role involves the youth sector and activities affecting children and young people, safeguarding responsibilities are particularly important. The successful applicant will be required to demonstrate a commitment to protecting children and young people. This includes: Participating in relevant safeguarding training Undergoing required Garda vetting Following child safeguarding policies and procedures Following relevant reporting arrangements Ensuring that the safety and wellbeing of young people remain paramount Candidates should therefore understand that safeguarding is a substantive professional responsibility attached to the position rather than merely an administrative recruitment requirement. Reporting Arrangements The successful Project Officer will report directly to the Youth 2030 Global Youth Work Programme Manager at the National Youth Council of Ireland. Overall accountability sits with the Director and Board of NYCI . This structure places the position within a wider programme and organisational accountability framework. Probationary and Notice Periods The position comes with a: Six-month probationary period and a: One-month notice period. Applicants should take these employment conditions into consideration when assessing the opportunity. Expected Starting Date NYCI expects the successful applicant to commence the role in: November 2026. Because recruitment is taking place during September 2026, shortlisted candidates should be prepared for a relatively quick appointment process. Recruitment Timeline and Interviews According to the live recruitment portal, shortlisted applicants are expected to be informed by 1 October 2026 , with face-to-face interviews anticipated during the week beginning 5 October 2026 . There is an inconsistency in NYCI’s separate vacancy announcement, which states that interviews are expected during the week beginning 12 October 2026 . Applicants should therefore remain available for further instructions from NYCI rather than relying exclusively on either indicative interview week. Application Process Applications must be completed through NYCI’s online recruitment system . The organisation clearly states that applications submitted through other methods will not be accepted. The application form requests substantial information from candidates, including educational background, professional training, employment history, voluntary experience, availability to take up the position, references, driving-licence status, and information demonstrating how the applicant meets the specific requirements of the role. Candidates are also asked whether they currently have the right to work in Ireland . Applicants should therefore allow sufficient time to complete the application carefully rather than treating it as a simple CV upload. The application form also asks for two referees , with one normally being the applicant’s current or most recent employer and at least one referee having knowledge of the candidate in a working environment, whether paid or unpaid. Apply for the NYCI Project Officer Position Applications can be submitted through the official NYCI recruitment portal: Apply for the Project Officer: Global Citizenship Education Trainer position Application Deadline Candidates should submit their applications no later than: 2:00 p.m., Monday, 28 September 2026 The live NYCI recruitment portal gives this as the deadline. NYCI’s accompanying news article instead states 5:00 p.m. on 28 September 2026 . Because the two official pages conflict and the recruitment portal is where applications are actually submitted, prospective applicants should use the earlier 2:00 p.m. deadline to avoid any risk of submitting too late. Why This Opportunity Stands Out The Project Officer: Global Citizenship Education Trainer position offers a distinctive combination of practical training, education, sustainable development, youth engagement, project management, stakeholder relations, research, and monitoring and evaluation. The successful applicant will not simply deliver workshops. They will contribute to strengthening the capacity of the wider youth sector to engage young people with some of the most important global issues of the present decade. The opportunity may be particularly meaningful for professionals who want their training and education experience to contribute directly to social justice, equality, sustainability, global citizenship, and youth participation. The position also offers the chance to work within an established national programme supported by Irish Aid and delivered with major organisations including Concern Worldwide, Trócaire, and Maynooth University. At the same time, the combination of a competitive salary, hybrid working, 27 days of annual leave, pension contributions, professional development support, and family-friendly working provisions strengthens the overall employment package. Conclusion The NYCI Project Officer: Global Citizenship Education Trainer 2026 position presents a significant professional opportunity for an experienced trainer or education practitioner seeking to advance Global Citizenship Education, Global Youth Work, sustainable development, and youth participation in Ireland. Based in Dublin and working within the Youth 2030 Global Youth Work Programme , the successful applicant will design and deliver training, develop educational resources, coordinate training activities, strengthen professional networks, build relationships with youth-sector stakeholders, contribute to monitoring and evaluation, and represent Youth 2030 within the wider Global Citizenship Education community. With an annual salary ranging from €35,779 to €48,408 , hybrid working, substantial annual leave, pension contributions, staff development opportunities, and a role directly connected with the Sustainable Development Goals, this position offers both professional development and an opportunity to contribute to meaningful social change. Candidates interested in applying should prepare their online application carefully and submit it through NYCI’s recruitment portal before 2:00 p.m. on Monday, 28 September 2026 .
